title: Observer-Dependent Observable Geometry
description: A topological model shows how unanimous observability depends strictly on channel architecture. Opposite one-sided observers on the real line have ordinary Euclidean geometry as their consensus, causing the half-open state $[0,1)$ to lose openness.
key_results: Channel-Addition Criterion: a region remains open after adding a channel exactly when it is open both for the new channel and for the old consensus.
Two-Channel Euclidean Collapse Theorem: the consensus of the lower-limit and upper-limit topologies on the real line is exactly the Euclidean topology.
Strict Observer-Dependence Theorem: the one-channel lower-limit geometry is strictly finer than the two-channel consensus geometry.
Half-Open State Collapse: $[0,1)$ is open for the lower-limit observer but not for the two-channel consensus.

# When More Eyes See Less: A Topological Model of Observer-Dependent Geometry

Imagine walking through a world in which every location has a preferred direction. From a point $x$, you can resolve what lies immediately to the right, but the left edge is blurred into the point itself. Your elementary windows of perception are not symmetric intervals $(a,b)$. They are half-open intervals

$$
[a,b)=\{x\in\mathbb R:a\le x<b\}.
$$

Now add a second observer whose directional bias is reversed. This observer sees through windows $(a,b]$. One might expect two channels to reveal every distinction available to either one. But unanimity changes the logic. If a region counts as observable only when *both* channels recognize it as open, then a feature visible to just one channel disappears from their shared geometry. Two perspectives can produce a coarser public world than one.

That reversal—more channels, fewer unanimously observable regions—is the central idea of an exact topological model of observer-dependent reality. It does not claim that spacetime literally changes when watched, nor that a brain is simply a collection of topologies. Rather, it isolates a rigorous mechanism by which the architecture of observation can condition the geometry of what is reportable.

## Geometry as a vocabulary of observable regions

A topology on a set $X$ is a collection $\mathcal T$ of subsets called open sets. It must contain $\varnothing$ and $X$, be closed under arbitrary unions, and be closed under finite intersections. These rules say that impossible and total observations are admissible, that alternatives can be combined, and that finitely many simultaneous observational conditions can be imposed.

Topology usually describes continuity and nearness. Here it plays another role: $U\in\mathcal T$ means that the region $U$ is resolvable by an observer channel. The topology is therefore a channel's vocabulary of stable, observable regions.

A perceptual network with $n$ channels on $X$ is a finite family

$$
(\mathcal T_0,\mathcal T_1,\ldots,\mathcal T_{n-1})
$$

of topologies on the same carrier. Its **consensus topology** consists of exactly those sets that are open for every channel:

$$
\mathcal C(\mathcal T_0,\ldots,\mathcal T_{n-1})
=\bigcap_{i=0}^{n-1}\mathcal T_i.
$$

This intersection is again a topology. Empty and total regions belong to every channel; unions remain open in every channel; and finite intersections do too. Thus unanimous observability has a coherent geometry of its own.

The consensus rule matters. It models conservative fusion: a region enters the shared observable state only if no channel vetoes it. Other fusion rules are possible, but this one exposes a clean collapse phenomenon.

## The one-sided observers

On the real line, consider the **lower-limit topology** $\mathcal L$. It is generated by the half-open intervals $[a,b)$. A set is $\mathcal L$-open when every one of its points lies in some interval $[a,b)$ contained in the set. This topology is finer than ordinary Euclidean topology: every usual open interval can be assembled from lower-limit basic intervals, but $[0,1)$ itself is lower-limit open and not Euclidean open.

Reflect the direction to obtain the **upper-limit topology** $\mathcal U$, generated by intervals $(a,b]$. It also contains all Euclidean-open sets, while admitting right-closed regions such as $(0,1]$ that ordinary geometry rejects as open.

A one-channel network using $\mathcal L$ has consensus exactly $\mathcal L$. This is the One-Channel Identity Theorem: the shared geometry of a single channel is simply that channel's geometry. In particular, $[0,1)$ is observable as an open state.

The more interesting system has two channels, one using $\mathcal L$ and the other using $\mathcal U$. Its shared open sets are those belonging to both:

$$
\mathcal C(\mathcal L,\mathcal U)=\mathcal L\cap\mathcal U.
$$

The Two-Channel Collapse Theorem says that this intersection is exactly the ordinary Euclidean topology $\mathcal E$.

Why? Every Euclidean-open set is open in both one-sided topologies. Conversely, suppose $V$ is open in both and $x\in V$. Lower-limit openness provides some $b>x$ with $[x,b)\subseteq V$. Upper-limit openness provides some $a<x$ with $(a,x]\subseteq V$. Putting these two directional certificates together gives

$$
(a,b)=(a,x]\cup[x,b)\subseteq V.
$$

So every point of $V$ has an ordinary open interval around it. Therefore $V$ is Euclidean open. Agreement between opposite one-sided resolutions restores two-sided local neighborhoods.

## A visible state that collapses

The interval $[0,1)$ makes the change tangible. Under the one-channel lower-limit network, it is a basic open region. Under the two-channel consensus, it is not open, because the consensus is Euclidean and no Euclidean neighborhood of $0$ remains inside $[0,1)$. The second channel does not erase the points of the interval. It changes the status of the interval as a stable observable region.

This distinction is essential. The carrier remains the same real line. No point is created or destroyed. What changes is the family of subsets licensed as open—the geometry of resolution.

The Strict Observer-Dependence Theorem can now be stated plainly: the one-channel observable geometry $\mathcal L$ is strictly finer than the two-channel observable geometry $\mathcal E$. Equivalently,

$$
\mathcal E\subsetneq\mathcal L.
$$

Consequently, finite networks of complexities one and two on the same underlying set can have unequal observable geometries. Complexity here means the number of channels, not computational power or biological sophistication. The theorem is structural: under unanimity, an added channel contributes an additional constraint.

## The law of adding a channel

The example reflects a general law. Let a network have consensus $\mathcal C$, and add a new channel with topology $\mathcal T$. Then a set $A$ is open in the enlarged network exactly when

$$
A\in\mathcal T\quad\text{and}\quad A\in\mathcal C.
$$

Hence the new consensus is

$$
\mathcal C'=\mathcal C\cap\mathcal T.
$$

This Channel-Addition Criterion immediately explains monotonicity. Adding a channel can preserve or remove shared open sets, but it cannot create one. Strict change occurs precisely when the new channel vetoes at least one set that all old channels accepted.

This logic resembles fault-tolerant systems, scientific replication, and multisensor fusion. A safety controller may act only on events recognized by every detector. A scientific claim may enter consensus only after surviving several methods. A legal or institutional decision may require unanimity. In each case, additional perspectives enlarge the body of private information while potentially shrinking the body of common certification.

Topology adds something distinctive to this familiar logic: the accepted events are not an arbitrary list. They obey closure laws, so they define continuity, convergence, neighborhoods, and boundaries. Changing consensus can therefore change which processes count as continuous and which states count as locally stable.

Consider a trajectory through the state space. Whether that trajectory appears smooth depends on which regions qualify as neighborhoods. When consensus removes open sets, it can alter the tests used to recognize continuity. The observer architecture therefore influences not only a static inventory of visible regions, but also the qualitative description of motion between them. This opens a route from perceptual geometry to dynamical models, where abrupt changes in agreement may register as changes in apparently smooth behavior.

## What the model does—and does not—say

The phrase “observer-dependent reality” invites grand interpretations, but the mathematics is more disciplined. The model proves a conditional statement: if channels are represented by topologies and shared observability means unanimous openness, then observable geometry depends on channel architecture, and it can change strictly when a channel is added.

It does not establish an empirical law of neural perception. To connect the framework to experiments, one would need a principled map from measurements or neural readouts to open sets. One possibility is to begin with distinguishability: a channel generates a topology from the state subsets it can reliably separate. The consensus then captures distinctions stable across all readouts. Whether biological or physical data behave this way is a falsifiable question, not a consequence of the model.

Nor does the result say that more observation always means less knowledge. The private outputs of the network may become richer. Only the unanimously certified geometry becomes coarser. If fusion used “accepted by at least one channel,” the behavior would differ, and the union of topologies would generally need closure operations before becoming a topology.

## From a line to networks of worlds

The real-line example is minimal but suggestive. On finite state spaces, one can list every channel's open sets and compute consensus by intersection. This makes it possible to search for the smallest number of observers needed to realize a target topology as common ground among finer private topologies. On product spaces, one can ask when combining two systems before consensus gives the same answer as taking consensus before forming the product. Those operations need not commute automatically.

A further direction replaces idealized channels with a finite transition graph. Nodes represent internal or physical states; a readout declares certain groups distinguishable; those groups generate a topology. Adding a readout then strictly changes consensus exactly when it rejects a region accepted by every previous readout. The prediction can be tested by finite enumeration.

The deepest lesson is not that observers magically manufacture points. It is that geometry can encode a protocol of agreement. A single directional eye admits $[0,1)$ as an open possibility. A second, oppositely directed eye demands a certificate from the other side, and the half-open state loses its privileged status. What survives is the familiar Euclidean line—not assumed in advance, but recovered as the common core of two asymmetric views.

In this model, reality is not merely what any observer can see. It is what a network has agreed to call open.

# Observer-Dependent Observable Geometry: Consensus, Channel Addition, and Collapse on the Real Line

**Aristotle**  
**August 1, 2026**

## Abstract

We present a self-contained topological model in which an observer channel is represented by a topology on a common state space and the geometry observable to a finite network is the intersection of its channel topologies. This intersection, called the consensus topology, contains exactly the regions certified as open by every channel. We prove a general channel-addition criterion: after adjoining a topology $\mathcal T$ to a network with consensus $\mathcal C$, a set is open precisely when it belongs to both $\mathcal T$ and $\mathcal C$. Consequently, adding channels can only coarsen consensus, and the coarsening is strict exactly when the new channel rejects an open set shared by all previous channels. On $\mathbb R$, a one-channel network using the lower-limit topology observes that topology itself, while a two-channel network combining the lower- and upper-limit topologies observes exactly the Euclidean topology. Thus network complexities one and two yield strictly different observable geometries on the same carrier. The half-open interval $[0,1)$ is a concrete witness: it is open for the one-channel network and ceases to be open after the second channel is imposed. We discuss finite algorithms, applications to conservative multisensor fusion, and the assumptions required before interpreting the construction as a model of physical or neural observation.

## 1. Introduction

Geometry is ordinarily assigned to a space independently of those who inspect it. Nevertheless, many operational settings do not expose all subsets of a state space equally. A sensor has a family of resolvable events, an experimental procedure has a family of robustly detectable conditions, and a readout mechanism has a family of stable distinctions. When several channels must agree before a region is accepted as observable, the resulting common vocabulary may have geometric structure.

Topology supplies a minimal language for this situation. A topology records which regions are open and thereby determines neighborhoods, continuity, convergence, and boundaries. We interpret each channel topology as a family of resolvable regions. For a finite network, we define the observable geometry by unanimity: a region is open for the network exactly when every channel regards it as open. The resulting family is the intersection of the individual topologies and is itself a topology.

This choice models conservative aggregation. It should be distinguished from pooling every region seen by at least one channel. Unanimity adds constraints: each new channel can veto a previously shared region. The direction of change is therefore opposite to the informal expectation that “more observers see more.” Private information may increase, but common certification can decrease.

The principal example uses two asymmetric topologies on the real line. The lower-limit topology is generated by intervals $[a,b)$ and resolves points from a right-facing perspective. Its reflected counterpart, the upper-limit topology, is generated by intervals $(a,b]$. Each is strictly finer than ordinary Euclidean topology. Yet their intersection is exactly Euclidean topology. A one-channel lower-limit network therefore recognizes $[0,1)$ as open, whereas a two-channel network requiring both one-sided observers to agree does not.

The result is a theorem about an explicit mathematical model. No empirical conclusion about spacetime, consciousness, or biological neural networks follows without an additional encoding that maps physical measurements to topological data. This distinction is central: the framework offers a rigorous conditional mechanism and a route to falsifiable finite models, not a claim that nature necessarily implements the mechanism.

The paper proceeds from definitions to general structural results, then to the real-line collapse, computational procedures, applications, limitations, and open directions.

## 2. Topological preliminaries

### 2.1 Topologies and comparison

Let $X$ be a set. A **topology** $\mathcal T$ on $X$ is a family of subsets of $X$ satisfying:

1. $\varnothing\in\mathcal T$ and $X\in\mathcal T$;
2. if $\{U_j\}_{j\in J}\subseteq\mathcal T$, then $\bigcup_{j\in J}U_j\in\mathcal T$;
3. if $U,V\in\mathcal T$, then $U\cap V\in\mathcal T$.

The members of $\mathcal T$ are called **open sets**. A topology $\mathcal T_1$ is **finer** than $\mathcal T_2$ if $\mathcal T_2\subseteq\mathcal T_1$; equivalently, every $\mathcal T_2$-open set is $\mathcal T_1$-open. It is **strictly finer** when the inclusion is proper. Finer topologies make more subsets open and therefore encode more local distinctions.

Some order-theoretic conventions reverse the written order on topologies. To avoid ambiguity, all comparisons in this paper are stated directly as inclusions between families of open sets.

### 2.2 Bases

A family $\mathcal B$ of subsets of $X$ is a **basis** for a topology if every point lies in a basis element and, whenever $x\in B_1\cap B_2$ with $B_1,B_2\in\mathcal B$, there exists $B_3\in\mathcal B$ such that $x\in B_3\subseteq B_1\cap B_2$. The generated topology consists of arbitrary unions of basis elements. Equivalently, $U$ is open if and only if each $x\in U$ lies in some $B\in\mathcal B$ with $B\subseteq U$.

### 2.3 Three topologies on the real line

The **Euclidean topology** $\mathcal E$ on $\mathbb R$ has the open intervals $(a,b)$ as a basis.

The **lower-limit topology** $\mathcal L$ has the intervals

$$
[a,b)=\{x\in\mathbb R:a\le x<b\},\qquad a<b,
$$

as a basis. Thus $U\in\mathcal L$ exactly when, for every $x\in U$, there exists $b>x$ such that $[x,b)\subseteq U$ after possibly choosing a basis interval whose left endpoint is at or below $x$. In particular, every basic interval $[a,b)$ is $\mathcal L$-open.

The **upper-limit topology** $\mathcal U$ is the reflected version, based on

$$
(a,b]=\{x\in\mathbb R:a<x\le b\},\qquad a<b.
$$

Each Euclidean interval can be expressed as a union of lower-limit basis intervals and also as a union of upper-limit basis intervals. Hence

$$
\mathcal E\subseteq\mathcal L
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\mathcal E\subseteq\mathcal U.
$$

Both inclusions are strict. For example, $[0,1)\in\mathcal L$ but $[0,1)\notin\mathcal E$, while $(0,1]\in\mathcal U$ but $(0,1]\notin\mathcal E$.

## 3. Perceptual networks and consensus

### Definition 3.1 (finite perceptual network)

Let $X$ be a set and let $n\ge 1$. A **finite perceptual network of complexity $n$** is a family

$$
\mathbf T=(\mathcal T_i)_{i=0}^{n-1}
$$

of topologies on $X$. The integer $n$ counts channels only; it is not a measure of algorithmic complexity, intelligence, or biological sophistication.

### Definition 3.2 (observable or consensus geometry)

The **observable geometry** of $\mathbf T$ is its consensus topology

$$
\operatorname{Con}(\mathbf T)=\bigcap_{i=0}^{n-1}\mathcal T_i.
$$

Thus a subset $A\subseteq X$ is consensus-open if and only if

$$
A\in\mathcal T_i\quad\text{for every }i\in\{0,\ldots,n-1\}.
$$

### Proposition 3.3 (consensus is a topology)

For every family of topologies $\mathbf T$ on $X$, the family $\operatorname{Con}(\mathbf T)$ is a topology on $X$.

**Proof sketch.** Every channel contains $\varnothing$ and $X$, so both belong to the intersection. If every $A_j$ is open in every channel, then $\bigcup_j A_j$ is open in every channel and hence in the intersection. If $A$ and $B$ are open in every channel, then $A\cap B$ is open in every channel. These are precisely the topology axioms. $\square$

### Proposition 3.4 (one-channel identity)

If $\mathbf T=(\mathcal T)$ has one channel, then

$$
\operatorname{Con}(\mathbf T)=\mathcal T.
$$

**Proof sketch.** Membership in the intersection over a singleton family is exactly membership in its sole member. $\square$

Applied to the one-channel network $\mathbf L=(\mathcal L)$ on $\mathbb R$, this gives

$$
\operatorname{Con}(\mathbf L)=\mathcal L.
$$

## 4. The channel-addition theorem

The consensus rule has a simple compositional law.

### Theorem 4.1 (channel-addition criterion)

Let $\mathbf T=(\mathcal T_i)_{i\in I}$ be any observer family on $X$, with consensus $\mathcal C=\bigcap_{i\in I}\mathcal T_i$. Adjoin one channel with topology $\mathcal S$. For every $A\subseteq X$,

$$
A\in\operatorname{Con}(\mathcal S,\mathbf T)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
A\in\mathcal S\ \text{and}\ A\in\mathcal C.
$$

Equivalently,

$$
\operatorname{Con}(\mathcal S,\mathbf T)=\mathcal S\cap\mathcal C.
$$

**Proof sketch.** If $A$ is open in the enlarged consensus, it is open in each indexed channel; evaluating this condition at the new channel gives $A\in\mathcal S$, and evaluating it at every old channel gives $A\in\mathcal C$. Conversely, if both conditions hold, then $A$ is open in the new channel and in every old channel, so it is open in the enlarged consensus. $\square$

### Corollary 4.2 (monotonicity under channel addition)

With the hypotheses of Theorem 4.1,

$$
\operatorname{Con}(\mathcal S,\mathbf T)\subseteq\operatorname{Con}(\mathbf T).
$$

**Proof sketch.** The enlarged consensus is $\mathcal S\cap\mathcal C$, which is contained in $\mathcal C$. $\square$

### Corollary 4.3 (strictness criterion)

The inclusion in Corollary 4.2 is strict if and only if there exists $A\subseteq X$ such that

$$
A\in\operatorname{Con}(\mathbf T)
\qquad\text{but}\qquad
A\notin\mathcal S.
$$

**Proof sketch.** By Theorem 4.1, exactly the old consensus-open sets that fail to belong to $\mathcal S$ are removed. If one exists, the inclusion is proper. If none exists, then $\mathcal C\subseteq\mathcal S$, so $\mathcal S\cap\mathcal C=\mathcal C$. $\square$

This criterion gives a witness-based interpretation of collapse. A strict change does not require comparing entire topologies abstractly; one need only exhibit a previously shared open set vetoed by the new channel.

## 5. Collapse from one-sided to Euclidean geometry

We now analyze a network on $\mathbb R$ with two channels:

$$
\mathbf B=(\mathcal L,\mathcal U).
$$

The first resolves lower-limit neighborhoods and the second resolves upper-limit neighborhoods.

### Lemma 5.1 (Euclidean opens survive both channels)

Every Euclidean-open subset of $\mathbb R$ is open in both $\mathcal L$ and $\mathcal U$. Therefore

$$
\mathcal E\subseteq\mathcal L\cap\mathcal U.
$$

**Proof sketch.** Let $V$ be Euclidean open and $x\in V$. Choose $\varepsilon>0$ with $(x-\varepsilon,x+\varepsilon)\subseteq V$. The lower-limit neighborhood $[x,x+\varepsilon)$ lies in $V$, proving lower-limit openness at $x$. The upper-limit neighborhood $(x-\varepsilon,x]$ lies in $V$, proving upper-limit openness. $\square$

### Lemma 5.2 (two one-sided certificates yield a Euclidean neighborhood)

If $V$ is open in both $\mathcal L$ and $\mathcal U$, then every $x\in V$ has an ordinary open interval $(a,b)$ satisfying

$$
x\in(a,b)\subseteq V.
$$

**Proof sketch.** Lower-limit openness gives a rightward interval $[x,b)\subseteq V$ for some $b>x$. Upper-limit openness gives a leftward interval $(a,x]\subseteq V$ for some $a<x$. Their union is $(a,b)$ and remains in $V$. $\square$

### Theorem 5.3 (two-channel Euclidean collapse)

The consensus of the lower- and upper-limit channels is exactly the Euclidean topology:

$$
\operatorname{Con}(\mathbf B)=\mathcal L\cap\mathcal U=\mathcal E.
$$

**Proof sketch.** Lemma 5.1 proves $\mathcal E\subseteq\mathcal L\cap\mathcal U$. If $V\in\mathcal L\cap\mathcal U$, Lemma 5.2 gives a Euclidean neighborhood around each point of $V$, so $V\in\mathcal E$. This proves the reverse inclusion. $\square$

The word “collapse” refers to the loss of one-sided open sets when consensus is imposed, not to a change in the underlying point set.

### Theorem 5.4 (strict observer dependence)

The observable geometry of the one-channel lower-limit network is strictly finer than that of the two-channel lower/upper network:

$$
\operatorname{Con}(\mathbf B)=\mathcal E
\subsetneq
\mathcal L=\operatorname{Con}(\mathbf L).
$$

**Proof sketch.** Proposition 3.4 identifies the one-channel consensus with $\mathcal L$, and Theorem 5.3 identifies the two-channel consensus with $\mathcal E$. The inclusion $\mathcal E\subseteq\mathcal L$ holds by Lemma 5.1. It is strict because $[0,1)$ is lower-limit open but not Euclidean open. $\square$

### Corollary 5.5 (complexity changes the observable geometry)

There exist finite perceptual networks of complexities one and two on the same carrier $\mathbb R$ whose observable geometries are unequal.

**Proof sketch.** The networks $\mathbf L$ and $\mathbf B$ have respective consensus topologies $\mathcal L$ and $\mathcal E$, which are unequal by Theorem 5.4. $\square$

### Corollary 5.6 (half-open state collapse)

The region $[0,1)$ is open in the observable geometry of $\mathbf L$ and is not open in the observable geometry of $\mathbf B$.

**Proof sketch.** The set is a basic element of $\mathcal L$. In Euclidean topology it is not open because every ordinary neighborhood of $0$ contains negative points and therefore cannot be contained in $[0,1)$. Apply Proposition 3.4 and Theorem 5.3. $\square$

## 6. Algorithms and numerical demonstrations

The real-line proof is symbolic, but finite samples can make its mechanism visible. On a grid

$$
G=\{-mh,\ldots,-h,0,h,\ldots,mh\},
$$

one may represent a region by a bit mask. Families of candidate lower, upper, and symmetric intervals are generated from grid endpoints. Consensus acceptance is then computed by logical conjunction of channel predicates.

### Algorithm 6.1 (finite consensus intersection)

**Input:** A finite carrier $X$ and channel topologies $\mathcal T_1,\ldots,\mathcal T_n$, each stored as a set of immutable subsets of $X$.

**Output:** The consensus topology $\mathcal C$.

**Procedure:** Initialize $\mathcal C=\mathcal T_1$. For $i=2,\ldots,n$, replace $\mathcal C$ by $\mathcal C\cap\mathcal T_i$. Return $\mathcal C$.

If each topology is stored as a hash set and contains at most $M$ open subsets, the expected running time is $O(nM)$ membership operations, apart from subset encoding costs. Since a topology on a $q$-point carrier may contain up to $2^q$ opens, explicit enumeration is inherently exponential in $q$ in the worst case.

### Algorithm 6.2 (strict-collapse witness search)

**Input:** An old consensus $\mathcal C$ and a new channel topology $\mathcal S$ on a finite carrier.

**Output:** Either a witness $A\in\mathcal C\setminus\mathcal S$ or a report that consensus is unchanged.

**Procedure:** Iterate through $A\in\mathcal C$. If $A\notin\mathcal S$, return $A$. If the scan ends, return “unchanged.”

The expected running time is $O(|\mathcal C|)$ hash lookups. Correctness follows directly from Corollary 4.3.

### Interpreting a grid demonstration

A finite grid does not literally inherit the three infinite topologies merely by clipping intervals; endpoint effects and discretization can alter openness. The numerical demonstration should therefore be read as an illustration of channel predicates and witness loss, not as a substitute for Theorem 5.3. It confirms the intended directional behavior: $[0,1)$ matches a lower-limit basic region, fails the Euclidean neighborhood test at $0$, and is vetoed by the upper-facing channel.

For a direct finite model, one should instead specify actual topologies on a finite set and check the topology axioms. Their consensus is then exact and can be enumerated without approximation.

## 7. Applications and interpretation

### 7.1 Conservative multisensor fusion

Suppose each sensor certifies a family of stable state regions. If a controller acts only when every sensor certifies the same region, its operational event structure is the consensus topology. Adding a sensor cannot create a unanimously certified event. It either preserves consensus or removes events that the new sensor cannot certify.

This is useful when false positives are costly. The strictness criterion identifies exactly what changed: each lost open set is a concrete disagreement witness. In the real-line model, $[0,1)$ is accepted by a right-resolving channel but rejected once a left-resolving requirement is added.

### 7.2 Neural and perceptual state models

For a finite neural-state transition graph, a readout channel could be assigned a topology generated by state subsets that it reliably distinguishes. Multiple readouts would then induce a consensus geometry. Such an encoding must be justified by data: one must specify what counts as distinguishability, how noise affects generators, and why unanimity is the correct fusion rule.

If these choices are made, Corollary 4.3 becomes experimentally testable. Adding a readout strictly coarsens consensus exactly when it rejects a set accepted by every prior readout. The claim can be falsified by exhibiting a readout table for which the predicted and computed intersections disagree.

### 7.3 Shared scientific observability

Different experimental modalities may support different stable event families. Their common topology represents conditions robust across all modalities. The model separates two ideas often conflated in discussions of evidence: the union of everything detected somewhere and the intersection of what survives every protocol. Consensus concerns the latter.

### 7.4 Continuity under consensus

Because consensus changes a topology, it also changes continuity. If the topology on an observed state space becomes coarser, continuity conditions for maps *into* that space generally become easier, while continuity conditions for maps *out of* it generally become harder. Thus channel architecture may alter not only which regions are open but which transformations count as observationally smooth. This consequence follows from standard definitions of continuity and motivates studying dynamics over consensus geometries.

## 8. Limitations

First, the consensus rule is a modeling decision. Majority voting, weighted fusion, confidence thresholds, and union-based pooling produce different structures. A raw union of topologies need not itself be a topology, so disjunctive fusion requires taking the topology generated by the pooled opens.

Second, channel count is only a rudimentary complexity measure. Two identical channels have the same consensus as one; a single finely resolving channel may contain far more open sets than many coarse channels. The present result demonstrates strict dependence in a concrete pair of networks, not a universal law that every increase in channel number changes geometry.

Third, topology suppresses metric and probabilistic information. It records stable qualitative resolution but not distances, likelihoods, response times, or error rates. Empirical applications may require enriched structures such as uniform spaces, measures, filtrations, or sheaves.

Fourth, the real-line example is idealized. The lower- and upper-limit topologies encode perfect directional asymmetry. Physical sensors have finite precision and noise. A realistic model would use finite generated topologies or probabilistic neighborhoods and investigate the stability of consensus under perturbation.

Finally, the mathematical theorem does not imply that physical spacetime changes with observation. It says that the topology designated as unanimously observable depends on the family of channel topologies. Any ontological interpretation requires premises external to the theorem.

## 9. Further research

Several concrete directions follow.

1. **Finite observer-complexity monotonicity.** For a network indexed by $n$ channels and an extension by one agreeing with the original channels on their indices, prove inclusion of the new consensus in the old one in a uniform finite-index notation. The set-theoretic content is Corollary 4.2; the aim is a reusable indexed formulation.

2. **Strictness under extension.** Develop witness extraction procedures for the equivalence between strict consensus loss and the existence of an old shared open set rejected by the new channel. On finite spaces, these witnesses are computable.

3. **Minimal observer complexity.** For a finite carrier $X$ and target topology $\mathcal T$, define the least $n$ such that $\mathcal T$ is the consensus of $n$ strict refinements. Investigate bounds in terms of $|\mathcal T|$, the number of open sets. Exhaustive enumeration for carriers of size at most four is feasible.

4. **Product compositionality.** Given channel families on $X$ and $Y$ with a common index set, compare the consensus of channelwise product topologies with the product of the two consensus topologies. Characterizing equality would clarify when independent systems can be fused componentwise.

5. **Empirical encoding.** Given a measured finite transition graph and readout table, generate each readout topology from distinguishable subsets. Test whether adding a readout changes consensus exactly when it excludes a previously common open set.

6. **Approximate consensus.** Replace unanimity by acceptance from at least $k$ of $n$ channels. The resulting family of accepted sets need not be a topology, so one may study its topological closure or use a simplicial or sheaf-theoretic representation of partial agreement.

7. **Dynamic channels.** Let channel topologies vary with time and study discontinuities in the consensus path. A single channel crossing a witness threshold can trigger an abrupt topological change even when its parameters vary continuously in another sense.

## 10. Discussion

The lower/upper example shows that ordinary Euclidean geometry can arise as common ground between two non-Euclidean, directionally biased resolutions. This is not an averaging process. No metric midpoint is taken, and no probability is assigned. The operation is logical conjunction at the level of open sets.

That distinction explains both the simplicity and force of the result. Each one-sided topology contains Euclidean topology, so all ordinary opens survive. A region with only a right-facing local certificate may belong to $\mathcal L$ but fail in $\mathcal U$; a region with only a left-facing certificate behaves oppositely. The sets surviving both channels possess two-sided certificates at every point, and those certificates combine into ordinary open intervals.

The half-open interval $[0,1)$ is an especially informative witness because its failure is localized at one endpoint. Every interior point behaves ordinarily. At $0$, however, lower-limit geometry permits a neighborhood that begins exactly at the point and extends rightward. Euclidean geometry demands room on both sides. The upper-limit channel supplies the missing demand, and unanimity removes the half-open region from the public topology.

More generally, consensus topology is a geometry of common certification. Its monotonicity is not a paradox once private and shared observability are separated. Adding a channel increases the list of tests, while the family of regions passing all tests can only shrink. The result therefore belongs to a broad class of antitone relationships between constraints and feasible sets.

## 11. Conclusion

A finite observer network on a state space $X$ can be modeled as a family of topologies, with observable geometry defined by their intersection. This construction is topologically valid and obeys an exact channel-addition law: a region remains observable after a channel is added if and only if it was previously observable and the new channel also declares it open.

On $\mathbb R$, a single lower-limit channel observes the lower-limit topology. Adding the reflected upper-limit channel changes consensus to ordinary Euclidean topology. The change is strict, as witnessed by $[0,1)$, which is open before the addition and not open afterward. Thus the same carrier supports networks of different finite complexities with genuinely different observable geometries.

The model's contribution is a precise conditional mechanism for observer dependence. It does not turn observation into metaphysics; it turns agreement into topology. That mechanism is simple enough to compute on finite spaces, rich enough to affect continuity and local structure, and explicit enough to be tested whenever an empirical encoding of channel observability is supplied.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Numerical illustrations of consensus topology and one-sided collapse.

The finite example computes exact intersections of explicitly listed topologies.
The real-line example samples local neighborhoods to illustrate why [0, 1) is
lower-limit open but not Euclidean open. No third-party packages are required.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import FrozenSet, Iterable, Sequence, TypeVar

T = TypeVar("T")
FiniteSet = FrozenSet[T]
Topology = FrozenSet[FiniteSet[T]]


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ProbeResult:
    """Result of testing a neighborhood around one sampled point."""

    point: float
    lower_neighborhood: tuple[float, float]
    lower_fits: bool
    symmetric_neighborhood: tuple[float, float]
    symmetric_fits: bool


def powerset(items: Sequence[T]) -> list[FiniteSet[T]]:
    """Return every subset of a short finite sequence as a frozenset."""
    result: list[FiniteSet[T]] = []
    for mask in range(1 << len(items)):
        result.append(
            frozenset(items[index] for index in range(len(items)) if mask & (1 << index))
        )
    return result


def is_topology(carrier: FiniteSet[T], family: Topology[T]) -> bool:
    """Check the topology axioms by exhaustive finite enumeration."""
    empty: FiniteSet[T] = frozenset()
    if empty not in family or carrier not in family:
        return False
    # On a finite family, closure under binary unions implies arbitrary-union closure.
    for left in family:
        for right in family:
            if (left | right) not in family or (left & right) not in family:
                return False
    return True


def consensus(topologies: Sequence[Topology[T]]) -> Topology[T]:
    """Intersect the open-set families of all channels."""
    if not topologies:
        raise ValueError("At least one channel is required")
    shared = set(topologies[0])
    for topology in topologies[1:]:
        shared.intersection_update(topology)
    return frozenset(shared)


def collapse_witness(old_consensus: Topology[T], new_channel: Topology[T]) -> FiniteSet[T] | None:
    """Find an old consensus-open set vetoed by a new channel, if one exists."""
    rejected = old_consensus.difference(new_channel)
    if not rejected:
        return None
    return min(rejected, key=lambda subset: (len(subset), tuple(sorted(map(str, subset)))))


def in_half_open_unit_interval(x: float) -> bool:
    """Membership predicate for [0, 1)."""
    return 0.0 <= x < 1.0


def probe_half_open_interval(points: Iterable[float], radius: float = 0.1) -> list[ProbeResult]:
    """Sample directional and symmetric neighborhoods inside [0, 1).

    For each point x, the lower-limit test uses [x, x + delta), while the
    Euclidean test uses (x - delta, x + delta). Endpoint containment is tested
    numerically using representative points just inside each neighborhood.
    """
    if radius <= 0.0:
        raise ValueError("radius must be positive")
    results: list[ProbeResult] = []
    for x in points:
        delta = min(radius, max((1.0 - x) / 2.0, radius / 1000.0))
        lower = (x, x + delta)
        symmetric = (x - delta, x + delta)
        lower_samples = (x, x + delta / 2.0, x + 0.999 * delta)
        symmetric_samples = (x - 0.999 * delta, x, x + 0.999 * delta)
        results.append(
            ProbeResult(
                point=x,
                lower_neighborhood=lower,
                lower_fits=all(in_half_open_unit_interval(y) for y in lower_samples),
                symmetric_neighborhood=symmetric,
                symmetric_fits=all(in_half_open_unit_interval(y) for y in symmetric_samples),
            )
        )
    return results


def format_subset(subset: FiniteSet[str]) -> str:
    """Format a finite subset deterministically."""
    return "{" + ", ".join(sorted(subset)) + "}"


def run_finite_example() -> None:
    """Compute an exact strict consensus collapse on a three-state carrier."""
    carrier: FiniteSet[str] = frozenset({"left", "center", "right"})
    empty: FiniteSet[str] = frozenset()
    left = frozenset({"left"})
    left_center = frozenset({"left", "center"})
    right = frozenset({"right"})
    center_right = frozenset({"center", "right"})

    lower_like: Topology[str] = frozenset({empty, left, left_center, carrier})
    upper_like: Topology[str] = frozenset({empty, right, center_right, carrier})

    assert is_topology(carrier, lower_like)
    assert is_topology(carrier, upper_like)

    one_channel = consensus([lower_like])
    two_channel = consensus([lower_like, upper_like])
    witness = collapse_witness(one_channel, upper_like)

    print("EXACT FINITE CONSENSUS EXAMPLE")
    print(f"  one-channel open sets: {len(one_channel)}")
    print(f"  two-channel open sets: {len(two_channel)}")
    print("  consensus after adding the opposite channel:")
    for subset in sorted(two_channel, key=lambda s: (len(s), tuple(sorted(s)))):
        print(f"    {format_subset(subset)}")
    print(f"  strict-collapse witness: {format_subset(witness or empty)}")
    print()


def run_real_line_probe() -> None:
    """Display sampled neighborhood certificates for the key interval."""
    print("SAMPLED REAL-LINE NEIGHBORHOOD TEST FOR [0, 1)")
    for result in probe_half_open_interval([0.0, 0.25, 0.75], radius=0.1):
        print(
            f"  x={result.point:>4.2f}: "
            f"lower [x,b) fits={str(result.lower_fits):5s}; "
            f"symmetric (a,b) fits={str(result.symmetric_fits):5s}"
        )
    print("  At x=0, every positive-radius symmetric neighborhood reaches below 0.")
    print("  Thus [0,1) has a lower-limit certificate there, but no Euclidean one.")


def main() -> None:
    """Run all demonstrations."""
    run_finite_example()
    run_real_line_probe()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

algorithms.name: Finite Consensus Intersection with Strict-Collapse Witness Extraction
algorithms.description: Given explicitly represented finite channel topologies, the algorithm intersects their open-set families to compute unanimous observable geometry, then scans the old consensus for a set rejected by a proposed new channel. With hash-set representations and at most $M$ opens per channel, consensus computation takes expected $O(nM)$ membership operations for $n$ channels; witness extraction takes expected $O(|\mathcal C|)$. Explicit topology representation can itself require $2^{|X|}$ subsets in the worst case.
algorithms.pseudocode:
INPUT: channel topologies T[1..n], optionally a new channel S
REQUIRE: n >= 1 and every T[i] is a topology on the same finite carrier X
1. C <- T[1]
2. FOR i <- 2 TO n:
3.     C <- C INTERSECTION T[i]
4. IF S is absent: RETURN C
5. FOR EACH region A IN C:
6.     IF A NOT IN S: RETURN (C INTERSECTION S, A)
7. RETURN (C, NO STRICT-COLLAPSE WITNESS)

interactive_layout:
# Guided Tour: When Agreement Changes Geometry

Begin with a simple shift in viewpoint: a topology is a vocabulary of regions an observer can resolve. On the real line, the lower-limit observer uses windows $[a,b)$, while the reflected upper-limit observer uses $(a,b]$. Neither view is ordinary Euclidean geometry, yet their unanimous common ground is exactly Euclidean.

[Learn more about the lower-limit topology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lower_limit_topology) and review the [definition of a topological space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_space).

## 1. Touch the endpoint

The interval $[0,1)$ is the decisive witness. A lower-limit neighborhood may begin at $0$ and extend rightward, but an ordinary neighborhood must extend on both sides. Use the controls below. First leave only the lower channel active at $x=0$; then add the upper channel.

{{interactive_demo:0}}

<details><summary>Reveal the local proof</summary>
For lower-limit geometry, $[0,1)$ is itself a basic open interval. For Euclidean geometry, suppose it were open. Then $0$ would have some neighborhood $(-arepsilon,arepsilon)$ contained in $[0,1)$, but $-arepsilon/2$ belongs to that neighborhood and not to $[0,1)$, a contradiction.
</details>

## 2. Turn many channels into one geometry

For channel topologies $\mathcal T_1,\ldots,\mathcal T_n$, define consensus by

$$
\mathcal C= igcap_{i=1}^n\mathcal T_i.
$$

The algorithm below performs this intersection exactly on finite spaces and searches for a witness removed by a newly added channel.

{{algorithm:0}}

<details><summary>Why is the intersection still a topology?</summary>
Every channel contains $arnothing$ and the whole state space. A union of sets open in every channel remains open in every channel, and the same holds for a finite intersection. Therefore the common family satisfies all topology axioms.
</details>

## 3. Watch strict collapse in a finite world

The executable demonstration constructs two exact topologies on a three-state carrier. Each has four opens, but their consensus contains only the empty set and the whole carrier. It then reports a set accepted before and vetoed after channel addition.

{{demo:0}}

The key distinction is between **private resolution** and **common certification**. More channels can contain more total information while fewer regions pass every test.

## 4. See the endpoint obstruction

The visualization makes the witness geometric. The points stay fixed; what changes is whether the highlighted subset qualifies as an open state.

{{visualization:0}}

<details><summary>Reveal the two-channel collapse theorem</summary>
Every Euclidean-open set is open in both one-sided topologies. Conversely, if $V$ is open in both and $x\in V$, lower-limit openness gives $[x,b)\subseteq V$ and upper-limit openness gives $(a,x]\subseteq V$. Their union is the ordinary interval $(a,b)\subseteq V$. Thus $V$ is Euclidean open, proving $\mathcal L\cap\mathcal U=\mathcal E$.
</details>

## 5. Carry the idea outward

A finite sensor or neural readout can be assigned a topology generated by the state subsets it distinguishes. The channel-addition law predicts strict change exactly when a new readout rejects a region accepted by all old readouts. This is a testable finite computation once the distinguishability data and fusion rule are specified.

For broader context, explore [multisensor data fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sensor_fusion) and the role of [initial and final topologies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Induced_topology) in transporting observational structure.

<details><summary>Expert caveat: what the model does not claim</summary>
The theorem is conditional on representing each channel by a topology and defining shared observability by unanimity. It does not establish that biological perception or physical spacetime obeys those premises. Majority fusion, uncertainty, metric precision, and temporal dynamics require richer models.
</details>

By the end of the tour, the apparent paradox should dissolve: adding a channel adds a constraint. Under unanimity, the geometry of agreement can only stay the same or become coarser.

import Novelty.PhantomTopology

/-!
# Observer-dependent observable geometry

This file gives a precise topological model of observer-dependent geometry.  It
builds directly on the catalog's `PhantomTopology` and `consensus`: a perceptual
network is indexed by its finite collection of observer channels, and its
observable geometry is their consensus topology.

The result is a theorem about this mathematical model, not an assertion that
physical spacetime or biological neural networks satisfy the model's premises.
The explicit one-channel and two-channel networks show strict dependence on
network complexity: the former observes the lower-limit topology, whereas the
latter observes ordinary Euclidean geometry.
-/

open Phantom

namespace ObserverDependentReality

/-- A finite perceptual network of topological complexity `n`, using the
catalog's observer-family representation. -/
abbrev PerceptualNetwork (n : ℕ) (X : Type*) := PhantomTopology (Fin n) X

/-- The observable geometric state is the unanimous topology already defined by
`Phantom.consensus`. -/
def observableGeometry {n : ℕ} {X : Type*} (N : PerceptualNetwork n X) :
    TopologicalSpace X :=
  consensus N

/-- The one-channel network whose sole channel uses the lower-limit topology. -/
def oneChannelNetwork : PerceptualNetwork 1 ℝ := fun _ => lowerTop

/-- The two-channel network transports the catalog's Bool-indexed observers
along the standard equivalence `Fin 2 ≃ Bool`. -/
def twoChannelNetwork : PerceptualNetwork 2 ℝ := fun i =>
  observersℝ (finTwoEquiv i)

/-- A one-channel network has exactly its channel's geometry as observable
state. -/
theorem oneChannel_observable :
    observableGeometry oneChannelNetwork = lowerTop := by
  rw [observableGeometry, consensus]
  exact iSup_const

/-- A set is observable after adjoining one further channel precisely when it
is visible both to that channel and to every old channel. -/
theorem option_channel_isOpen_iff {ι X : Type*}
    (N : PhantomTopology ι X) (t : TopologicalSpace X) (U : Set X) :
    (consensus (fun i : Option ι => Option.elim i t N)).IsOpen U ↔
      t.IsOpen U ∧ (consensus N).IsOpen U := by
  rw [consensus_isOpen_iff, consensus_isOpen_iff]
  constructor
  · intro h
    exact ⟨h none, fun i => h (some i)⟩
  · rintro ⟨ht, hN⟩ i
    cases i with
    | none => exact ht
    | some i => exact hN i

/-- The two-channel network's observable geometry is the Euclidean topology.
This is the collapse from two one-sided resolutions to their two-sided
consensus. -/
theorem twoChannel_observable :
    observableGeometry twoChannelNetwork =
      (inferInstance : TopologicalSpace ℝ) := by
  change (⨆ i : Fin 2, observersℝ (finTwoEquiv i)) = _
  rw [finTwoEquiv.iSup_comp, ← consensus, consensus_pair_eq_standard]

/-- **Strict observer dependence.** Increasing topological complexity from one
channel to two changes the observable geometric state strictly.  In Mathlib's
order on topologies, `<` means that the left topology is strictly finer. -/
theorem observable_strictly_conditioned :
    observableGeometry oneChannelNetwork <
      observableGeometry twoChannelNetwork := by
  rw [oneChannel_observable, twoChannel_observable]
  apply lt_of_le_of_ne
  · rw [← consensus_pair_eq_standard, consensus]
    exact le_iSup observersℝ true
  · exact lowerTop_ne_standard

/-- Consequently, the same carrier `ℝ` admits finite perceptual networks of
complexities one and two with unequal observable geometric states. -/
theorem complexity_changes_observable :
    observableGeometry oneChannelNetwork ≠
      observableGeometry twoChannelNetwork :=
  ne_of_lt observable_strictly_conditioned

/-- The concrete collapse is nontrivial: the half-open interval `[0,1)` is
visible to the one-channel observer but ceases to be open in the two-channel
observable geometry. -/
theorem halfOpen_state_collapses :
    (observableGeometry oneChannelNetwork).IsOpen (Set.Ico (0 : ℝ) 1) ∧
      ¬(observableGeometry twoChannelNetwork).IsOpen (Set.Ico (0 : ℝ) 1) := by
  rw [oneChannel_observable, twoChannel_observable]
  exact ⟨lowerOpen_Ico, not_isOpen_Ico⟩

end ObserverDependentReality

    (N : PhantomTopology ι X) (t : TopologicalSpace X) (U : Set X) :
    (consensus (fun i : Option ι => Option.elim i t N)).IsOpen U ↔
      t.IsOpen U ∧ (consensus N).IsOpen U := by
  rw [consensus_isOpen_iff, consensus_isOpen_iff]
  constructor
  · intro h
    exact ⟨h none, fun i => h (some i)⟩
  · rintro ⟨ht, hN⟩ i
    cases i with
    | none => exact ht
    | some i => exact hN i

/-- The two-channel network's observable geometry is the Euclidean topology.
This is the collapse from two one-sided resolutions to their two-sided
consensus. -/
theorem twoChannel_observable :
    observableGeometry twoChannelNetwork =
      (inferInstance : TopologicalSpace ℝ) := by
  change (⨆ i : Fin 2, observersℝ (finTwoEquiv i)) = _
  rw [finTwoEquiv.iSup_comp, ← consensus, consensus_pair_eq_standard]

/-- **Strict observer dependence.** Increasing topological complexity from one
channel to two changes the observable geometric state strictly.  In Mathlib's
order on topologies, `<` means that the left topology is strictly finer. -/
theorem observable_strictly_conditioned :
    observableGeometry oneChannelNetwork <
      observableGeometry twoChannelNetwork := by
  rw [oneChannel_observable, twoChannel_observable]
  apply lt_of_le_of_ne
  · rw [← consensus_pair_eq_standard, consensus]
    exact le_iSup observersℝ true
  · exact lowerTop_ne_standard

/-- Consequently, the same carrier `ℝ` admits finite perceptual networks of
complexities one and two with unequal observable geometric states. -/
theorem complexity_changes_observable :
    observableGeometry oneChannelNetwork ≠
      observableGeometry twoChannelNetwork :=
  ne_of_lt observable_strictly_conditioned

/-- The concrete collapse is nontrivial: the half-open interval `[0,1)` is
visible to the one-channel observer but ceases to be open in the two-channel
observable geometry. -/
theorem halfOpen_state_collapses :
    (observableGeometry oneChannelNetwork).IsOpen (Set.Ico (0 : ℝ) 1) ∧
      ¬(observableGeometry twoChannelNetwork).IsOpen (Set.Ico (0 : ℝ) 1) := by
  rw [oneChannel_observable, twoChannel_observable]
  exact ⟨lowerOpen_Ico, not_isOpen_Ico⟩

end ObserverDependentReality

# Future Directions

The Lean development proves statements inside a precise topological observer model. The following conjectures are concrete extensions of that model and do not assert an empirical law about biological perception without additional physical assumptions.

1. **Finite observer-complexity monotonicity.** For every type `X`, every `N : Fin n → TopologicalSpace X`, and every extension `N' : Fin (n+1) → TopologicalSpace X` whose first `n` channels agree with `N`, prove `consensus N' ≤ consensus N`. This is falsified by any explicit extension violating the topology-lattice inequality.

2. **Strictness criterion for channel addition.** Under the same setup, prove that `consensus N' < consensus N` if and only if there is a set open for every old channel but not open for the new channel. Either implication can be falsified by a finite topological-space counterexample.

3. **Finite-space minimal observer complexity.** For a finite carrier `X` and target topology `t`, define the least `n` for which `t` is the consensus of `n` strict refinements, and prove that this number is bounded by the number of open sets of `t`. Exhaustive enumeration of topologies on carriers of size at most four can test the proposed bound.

4. **Product compositionality.** Given observer families `N` on `X` and `M` on `Y` with a common finite index type, characterize when the consensus of the channelwise product topologies equals the product of `consensus N` and `consensus M`. A pair of finite spaces where these topologies differ would refute an unrestricted equality.

5. **Empirical encoding conjecture.** For a specified finite neural-state transition graph, assign each readout channel a topology generated by its distinguishable state subsets. Test whether adding a readout node strictly coarsens consensus exactly when that node excludes an open set shared by all previous readouts. A measured transition graph and readout table make this directly falsifiable by finite computation.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Numerical illustrations of consensus topology and one-sided collapse.

The finite example computes exact intersections of explicitly listed topologies.
The real-line example samples local neighborhoods to illustrate why [0, 1) is
lower-limit open but not Euclidean open. No third-party packages are required.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import FrozenSet, Iterable, Sequence, TypeVar

T = TypeVar("T")
FiniteSet = FrozenSet[T]
Topology = FrozenSet[FiniteSet[T]]


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ProbeResult:
    """Result of testing a neighborhood around one sampled point."""

    point: float
    lower_neighborhood: tuple[float, float]
    lower_fits: bool
    symmetric_neighborhood: tuple[float, float]
    symmetric_fits: bool


def powerset(items: Sequence[T]) -> list[FiniteSet[T]]:
    """Return every subset of a short finite sequence as a frozenset."""
    result: list[FiniteSet[T]] = []
    for mask in range(1 << len(items)):
        result.append(
            frozenset(items[index] for index in range(len(items)) if mask & (1 << index))
        )
    return result


def is_topology(carrier: FiniteSet[T], family: Topology[T]) -> bool:
    """Check the topology axioms by exhaustive finite enumeration."""
    empty: FiniteSet[T] = frozenset()
    if empty not in family or carrier not in family:
        return False
    # On a finite family, closure under binary unions implies arbitrary-union closure.
    for left in family:
        for right in family:
            if (left | right) not in family or (left & right) not in family:
                return False
    return True


def consensus(topologies: Sequence[Topology[T]]) -> Topology[T]:
    """Intersect the open-set families of all channels."""
    if not topologies:
        raise ValueError("At least one channel is required")
    shared = set(topologies[0])
    for topology in topologies[1:]:
        shared.intersection_update(topology)
    return frozenset(shared)


def collapse_witness(old_consensus: Topology[T], new_channel: Topology[T]) -> FiniteSet[T] | None:
    """Find an old consensus-open set vetoed by a new channel, if one exists."""
    rejected = old_consensus.difference(new_channel)
    if not rejected:
        return None
    return min(rejected, key=lambda subset: (len(subset), tuple(sorted(map(str, subset)))))


def in_half_open_unit_interval(x: float) -> bool:
    """Membership predicate for [0, 1)."""
    return 0.0 <= x < 1.0


def probe_half_open_interval(points: Iterable[float], radius: float = 0.1) -> list[ProbeResult]:
    """Sample directional and symmetric neighborhoods inside [0, 1).

    For each point x, the lower-limit test uses [x, x + delta), while the
    Euclidean test uses (x - delta, x + delta). Endpoint containment is tested
    numerically using representative points just inside each neighborhood.
    """
    if radius <= 0.0:
        raise ValueError("radius must be positive")
    results: list[ProbeResult] = []
    for x in points:
        delta = min(radius, max((1.0 - x) / 2.0, radius / 1000.0))
        lower = (x, x + delta)
        symmetric = (x - delta, x + delta)
        lower_samples = (x, x + delta / 2.0, x + 0.999 * delta)
        symmetric_samples = (x - 0.999 * delta, x, x + 0.999 * delta)
        results.append(
            ProbeResult(
                point=x,
                lower_neighborhood=lower,
                lower_fits=all(in_half_open_unit_interval(y) for y in lower_samples),
                symmetric_neighborhood=symmetric,
                symmetric_fits=all(in_half_open_unit_interval(y) for y in symmetric_samples),
            )
        )
    return results


def format_subset(subset: FiniteSet[str]) -> str:
    """Format a finite subset deterministically."""
    return "{" + ", ".join(sorted(subset)) + "}"


def run_finite_example() -> None:
    """Compute an exact strict consensus collapse on a three-state carrier."""
    carrier: FiniteSet[str] = frozenset({"left", "center", "right"})
    empty: FiniteSet[str] = frozenset()
    left = frozenset({"left"})
    left_center = frozenset({"left", "center"})
    right = frozenset({"right"})
    center_right = frozenset({"center", "right"})

    lower_like: Topology[str] = frozenset({empty, left, left_center, carrier})
    upper_like: Topology[str] = frozenset({empty, right, center_right, carrier})

    assert is_topology(carrier, lower_like)
    assert is_topology(carrier, upper_like)

    one_channel = consensus([lower_like])
    two_channel = consensus([lower_like, upper_like])
    witness = collapse_witness(one_channel, upper_like)

    print("EXACT FINITE CONSENSUS EXAMPLE")
    print(f"  one-channel open sets: {len(one_channel)}")
    print(f"  two-channel open sets: {len(two_channel)}")
    print("  consensus after adding the opposite channel:")
    for subset in sorted(two_channel, key=lambda s: (len(s), tuple(sorted(s)))):
        print(f"    {format_subset(subset)}")
    print(f"  strict-collapse witness: {format_subset(witness or empty)}")
    print()


def run_real_line_probe() -> None:
    """Display sampled neighborhood certificates for the key interval."""
    print("SAMPLED REAL-LINE NEIGHBORHOOD TEST FOR [0, 1)")
    for result in probe_half_open_interval([0.0, 0.25, 0.75], radius=0.1):
        print(
            f"  x={result.point:>4.2f}: "
            f"lower [x,b) fits={str(result.lower_fits):5s}; "
            f"symmetric (a,b) fits={str(result.symmetric_fits):5s}"
        )
    print("  At x=0, every positive-radius symmetric neighborhood reaches below 0.")
    print("  Thus [0,1) has a lower-limit certificate there, but no Euclidean one.")


def main() -> None:
    """Run all demonstrations."""
    run_finite_example()
    run_real_line_probe()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
